region_note: Written for canal-irrigated paddy land of the old Cauvery delta (about 30 m above sea level, heavy clay soils, roughly 1,000-1,200 mm of rain of which about half falls in October-December). Seasons follow TNAU's Crop Production Guide: kuruvai (June-September), samba (August-January), thaladi (October-February) and rice-fallow crops afterwards.

equipment.label: Tractor and puddler, or transplanting labour
Seed drill or ridger for dry-sown crops

market.label: Only crops with assured buying (paddy procurement centres)
Open to regulated-market crops with price risk

references.FAO56: Allen, R.G., Pereira, L.S., Raes, D., Smith, M. (1998). Crop evapotranspiration. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (Tables 11, 12, 17, 22).
references.FAO33: Doorenbos, J., Kassam, A.H. (1979). Yield response to water. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 33; updated in Steduto et al. (2012), FAO Paper 66.
references.FAO29: Ayers, R.S., Westcot, D.W. (1985). Water quality for agriculture. FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29, Table 4 (crop salt tolerance).
references.TNAU: Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore. Crop Production Guide (Agriculture) and the TNAU Agritech Portal: seasons, varieties and durations for the Cauvery delta zone.
references.TRRI: Tamil Nadu Rice Research Institute, Aduthurai (TNAU): rice-fallow pulses and rice-fallow cotton recommendations for the delta.
references.METTUR: Water Resources Department, Government of Tamil Nadu: the Mettur (Stanley) reservoir is customarily opened for delta irrigation on 12 June; in years of low storage the opening is delayed and the kuruvai crop is cut back.
references.SARE: Clark, A. (ed.) (2007). Managing Cover Crops Profitably, 3rd edition. SARE Handbook 9 (legume nitrogen, green manures).
references.PROJECT: Class score assigned by this project from the general agronomy cited alongside it; not locally calibrated.

water.label: Save water
water.plain: Less irrigation water needed across the whole year.

cover.label: Keep soil covered
cover.plain: Crop or residue on the ground when the heavy rains arrive.

nitrogen.label: Nitrogen from legumes
nitrogen.plain: Nitrogen fixed by pulses and green manure and used by the rice.

organic_matter.label: Build organic matter
organic_matter.plain: Roots, residue and green manure returned to the soil.

pest_break.label: Break pest cycles
pest_break.plain: A break from rice after rice, with other plant families in between.

income.label: Income and assured sale
income.plain: Crop value relative to two rice crops, given your water and how you sell.

resilience.label: Heat and dry-spell resilience
resilience.plain: Crops that cope if canal water comes late or the monsoon fails.

feasibility.label: Easy to carry out
feasibility.plain: Fits your season, machinery and experience.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: rice Kc 1.05 initial, 1.20 mid-season, 0.90-0.60 late; a 105-110 day crop transplanted in June (TNAU).
why.cover: Flooded canopy June-September; stubble, soon puddled again, in October.
why.drought_tolerance: Grown in the hot, dry south-west monsoon months almost entirely on canal water: if the Mettur opening is late or flows are low, this crop fails or is not planted (METTUR).
why.establishment_risk: Depends on the reservoir opening on time (METTUR).
why.value_score: With the thaladi crop this makes up the reference income (0.50 + 0.50 = 1.0). Bought at direct purchase centres at the support price.
why.extra_water_mm: Puddling and keeping the field flooded take roughly 400-600 mm beyond what the crop transpires; in heavy delta clay less seeps away than in lighter soils (PROJECT estimate from FAO56 chapter on paddy).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12 rice values on a 130-135 day crop transplanted in October (TNAU).
why.drought_tolerance: Grown through the north-east monsoon, so rain supplies much of its water; the risk is flooding in November-December rather than drought.
why.establishment_risk: Young seedlings can be submerged by cyclonic rain in November.
why.value_score: Half of the reference income; assured purchase.
why.extra_water_mm: As for kuruvai rice, a little less because the season is wet and cool (PROJECT).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12 rice values on a 150-160 day crop planted in August-September (TNAU).
why.drought_tolerance: Most of its season falls in the north-east monsoon; needs canal water mainly to establish.
why.value_score: One long crop yields more than either short crop but less than two (PROJECT class score). Assured purchase.
why.om_score: A long crop leaves more root and stubble than a short one.

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: green gram and similar pulses Kc 0.4 initial, 1.05 mid-season, 0.6-0.35 late. Broadcast into the standing rice a week before harvest and grown on the moisture left in the soil, with no irrigation (TRRI), so it adds nothing to irrigation need.
why.n_score: A legume: fixes nitrogen and leaves a modest amount for the next rice crop (SARE; TRRI).
why.value_score: Low and variable yields (often 300-500 kg/ha) but almost no cost.
why.establishment_risk: Depends entirely on residual moisture and on January-February rain; yellow mosaic virus is common (TRRI).

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: cotton Kc 0.35 initial, 1.15-1.20 mid-season, 0.70-0.50 late, on the short rice-fallow season (TRRI).
why.drought_tolerance: Deep taproot (Ky 0.85, FAO33), but it grows through the hottest, driest months on borewell water.
why.value_score: A real cash crop in the delta, sold through regulated markets at prices that swing.
why.establishment_risk: Sown into wet rice stubble; summer showers and sucking pests decide the crop.

millet.label: Kuruvai-season maize or millet (instead of rice)

why.kc: FAO56 Table 12: maize Kc mid-season 1.20, millet 1.00; an in-between value is used for a 100-110 day crop with no puddling or standing water.
why.drought_tolerance: Can be raised with a few irrigations from a borewell when canal water is late (TNAU alternative-crop advice for delayed-water years).
why.value_score: Worth clearly less than a rice crop and has no assured buyer (PROJECT class score).
why.establishment_risk: Heavy delta clay drains slowly; these crops suffer if the field floods.

green_manure.label: Green manure (daincha or sunn hemp, ploughed in)

why.kc: Treated as a legume canopy (FAO56 Table 12 pulses) for the 45-50 days before it is ploughed in.
why.n_score: A 45-day stand ploughed in before transplanting supplies roughly 40-80 kg N/ha to the rice (TNAU; SARE).
why.om_score: All of its growth goes back into the soil.
why.value_score: No sale crop: its return is the fertiliser saved and the soil built.
why.drought_tolerance: Needs summer showers or one or two irrigations to establish.

kuruvai_thaladi_pulse.name: Kuruvai rice, thaladi rice and a rice-fallow pulse
kuruvai_thaladi_pulse.summary: Two rice crops a year (June-September and October-February), then blackgram on leftover moisture.
benefits: Two assured rice crops: the highest income when canal water arrives on time.
A pulse at almost no cost adds a little nitrogen and food.
The system the delta's canals, labour and markets are built around.
risks: The kuruvai crop depends on the Mettur reservoir opening on time and on borewells when it does not.
Rice after rice builds up stem borer, leaf folder and brown planthopper, and puddles the soil twice a year.
Thaladi seedlings can be drowned by cyclonic rain in November.
info_gaps: How often canal water reached your village by mid-June in the last ten years.
Whether you have a borewell, and its water quality.
verify: Ask the Public Works Department section office or the water users' association about this year's release schedule.
Ask TNAU extension or the KVK which short-duration variety suits a late start.

samba_pulse.name: One samba rice crop and a rice-fallow pulse
samba_pulse.summary: A single long-duration rice crop from August to January, then blackgram; the land rests in summer.
benefits: Needs canal water only from August, so a late Mettur opening matters much less.
Most of the crop's water comes from the north-east monsoon.
Half the puddling and a long break from rice pests.
risks: One rice crop earns clearly less than two.
The field lies bare through the hot months from April to July.
The whole year rides on one crop and on the north-east monsoon.
info_gaps: Whether summer showers are enough here to grow a green manure in the gap.
verify: Compare your own income from single and double cropping over wet and dry years.

samba_pulse_greenmanure.name: Samba rice, rice-fallow pulse and a summer green manure
samba_pulse_greenmanure.summary: As above, with daincha or sunn hemp grown in May-July and ploughed in before the samba crop.
benefits: Two legumes a year: the most nitrogen and organic matter of the options here.
The soil is covered in early summer instead of lying bare.
Still needs canal water only from August.
risks: The green manure needs summer showers or a borewell irrigation to establish.
One rice crop earns less than two; the green manure itself earns nothing.
Ploughing in has to be done on time, about ten days before transplanting.
info_gaps: Whether daincha or sunn hemp seed is available and subsidised this year.
verify: Ask the agriculture extension centre about green-manure seed supply.
Use a soil test to see how much fertiliser the green manure lets you cut.

millet_thaladi_pulse.name: Maize or millet in kuruvai, then thaladi rice and a pulse
millet_thaladi_pulse.summary: A dry-sown maize or millet replaces the kuruvai rice; thaladi rice and blackgram follow.
benefits: The June-September crop no longer needs standing water or an on-time canal.
Keeps one assured rice crop and the land in use all year.
A different plant group breaks the rice-after-rice pest cycle.
risks: Heavy delta clay drains slowly: maize and millets suffer if the field floods.
No assured buyer at a support price for the kuruvai-season crop.
Needs dry-land sowing equipment that paddy farms may not own.
info_gaps: Whether your field drains well enough for an upland crop in July-August.
Local buyers and prices for maize or millets.
verify: Ask TNAU extension about the alternative-crop package offered in delayed-water years.
Try it on your best-drained field first.

samba_cotton.name: Samba rice and rice-fallow cotton
samba_cotton.summary: A single samba rice crop, then cotton from February to June on borewell water.
benefits: A cash crop in the months when the canals are dry.
A deep-rooted crop from a different family; tolerates salty water better than rice.
risks: Cotton needs irrigation through the hottest months, from a borewell: it shifts water use to groundwater.
Prices and yields swing; sucking pests are common.
No pulse in the rotation, so no legume nitrogen.
info_gaps: Last season's cotton price at the regulated market.
verify: Check borewell water quality before relying on it for cotton.
Ask the Tamil Nadu Rice Research Institute about rice-fallow cotton varieties and sowing dates.

always_verify: This year's Mettur opening date and the canal turn schedule for your village.
A soil test (organic carbon, pH, salinity, nutrients), especially near the coast and at the tail end of canals.
Which crops are being bought at support prices this season, and where.
Varieties and sowing windows in the current TNAU Crop Production Guide.
